n: The chronicler steps back in time to show how warriors joined David even while he was hiding from Saul at Ziklag, a Philistine-granted town. Support for God’s chosen king grew steadily.

f.g: Stayed in hiding; lived in restricted circumstances.

n: The first to come were ambidextrous archers and slingers from Benjamin—Saul’s own tribe. Even Saul’s relatives recognized that God was with David.

f.w: both the right hand and the left

f.g: Saul’s fellow tribesmen and possibly relatives.

n: Their leaders are named, some from Saul’s hometown of Gibeah and from Anathoth.

f.g: From Gibeah, Saul’s capital.

n: Ismaiah from Gibeon was a leader among the Thirty.

f.g: David’s elite band of warriors (1 Chronicles 11:10-47).

n: More Benjamite warriors who joined David.

f.g: Possibly from a clan or place called Hariph (Nehemiah 7:24).

n: These were Korahites—Levites descended from Korah, perhaps living among Benjamin—who also came to David.

f.g: Korahites, descendants of Korah the Levite (1 Chronicles 9:19).

n: Two sons of Jeroham from Gedor complete the Benjamite list.

f.g: A town, perhaps in Benjamin or Judah.

n: Gadite warriors from east of the Jordan joined David in the wilderness. They are described with vivid images: faces like lions and feet as swift as gazelles.

f.g: David’s stronghold in the wilderness.
Gazelles or deer.

n: The Gadite leaders are listed in order of rank.

f.g: First in rank among the Gadite captains.

n: The fourth and fifth Gadite captains.

f.g: Meaning possibly “fatness” or “strength.”

n: The sixth and seventh captains.

f.g: “My God is God.”

n: The eighth and ninth captains.

f.g: “God has given.”

n: The tenth and eleventh captains complete the list.

f.g: A Gadite captain mentioned only here.

n: These Gadites became army commanders; even the least of them could lead a hundred, the greatest a thousand.

f.w: one of the least was over an hundred
f.g: Or, “one of them could stand against a hundred”—the Hebrew can read either way.

n: They crossed the Jordan in spring flood season—a dangerous feat—and drove off enemies on both sides of the valley.

f.g: Nisan (March–April), when snowmelt swelled the Jordan.

n: Men from Benjamin and Judah also came to David’s stronghold.

f.g: Men from both David’s tribe and Saul’s.

n: David wisely tests their motives: if you come in peace, I will welcome you with all my heart; if you come to betray me, let God judge you.

f.w: mine heart shall be knit unto you
f.g: I will be bound to you in loyal friendship.
Judge and punish it.

n: The Spirit inspires Amasai to pledge loyalty in poetic words: “We are yours, David… peace to you, for your God helps you.” David welcomes them as officers.

f.g: Literally “the Spirit clothed Amasai”—filling him to speak inspired words.

n: Some men of Manasseh defected to David when he marched with the Philistines toward Saul’s final battle. The Philistine rulers distrusted David and sent him away—sparing him from fighting Israel.

f.w: the lords of the Philistines upon advisement sent him away

f.g: After consulting together.

n: On his way back to Ziklag, seven commanders from Manasseh joined him.

f.g: Officers each commanding a large military unit.

n: They helped David fight the Amalekite raiders who had burned Ziklag and taken his family.

f.g: The raiding party—the Amalekites.

n: Day after day more people came until David’s force was like the army of God—a hint that heaven was behind this growing movement.

f.g: An idiom for something very great; also suggests divine support.

n: Now the chronicler lists the warriors who came to Hebron to make David king, as the Lord had promised.

f.w: according to the word of the LORD

n: Judah sent 6,800 armed men.

f.g: Heavily armed infantry.

n: Simeon sent 7,100 warriors.

f.g: A small southern tribe closely tied to Judah.

n: Even the Levites, normally temple servants, sent 4,600 men.

f.g: Levites were not usually counted for war (Numbers 1:47-49); here they show support for David.

n: Jehoiada led the priestly descendants of Aaron, with 3,700 men.

f.g: Descendants of Aaron—the priestly families.

n: Zadok, a brave young man, came with twenty-two family commanders. He would later become David’s high priest.
Only 3,000 came from Benjamin, since most of Saul’s tribe had remained loyal to his house until then.

f.w: kept the ward of the house of Saul
f.g: Remained loyal to and guarded Saul’s family’s interests.

n: Ephraim sent 20,800 renowned warriors.

f.w: famous throughout the house of their fathers
f.g: Well known in their clans.

n: The western half-tribe of Manasseh sent 18,000, each one named and chosen for the task.

f.g: Specifically designated by name.

n: Issachar’s leaders were valued for wisdom: they “understood the times” and knew what Israel should do. Discernment can be as valuable as strength.

f.g: Insight into current events and what the moment required.

n: Zebulun sent 50,000 skilled soldiers who were completely loyal—“not of double heart.”

f.g: Stay in battle formation; disciplined.
Single-minded; wholehearted in loyalty.

n: Naphtali sent a thousand officers with 37,000 men.

f.g: A northern tribe around the Sea of Galilee.

n: Dan sent 28,600 skilled fighters.

f.g: Members of the tribe of Dan, by now mostly in the far north (Judges 18).

n: Asher sent 40,000 trained soldiers.

f.g: A tribe along the northern Mediterranean coast.

n: The tribes east of the Jordan sent 120,000. The large numbers stress that the whole nation, near and far, embraced David.

f.w: on the other side of Jordan
f.g: East of the Jordan River.

n: All these came “with a perfect heart”—wholehearted—to make David king, and all Israel was of one mind. Unity around God’s chosen leader is the chronicler’s ideal.

f.g: A whole, undivided, sincere heart.

n: They feasted with David for three days, supplied by their fellow Israelites.

f.g: A covenant celebration meal, sealing the new relationship.

n: Even the far northern tribes sent food on every kind of animal. The chapter ends with joy—what unity under God’s king brings.

f.g: Pressed fig cakes, a durable food for travel.
